# The Credentialing Interface {#sec-3-06}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act II — Hoover, War, and the Archive State · 1919–1929
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does an institution become a bridge between private money
and public authority?

**The answer.** By becoming the place where private money and public authority
have to meet. Through the 1920s Stanford stopped being merely a good university
and became a switchboard: donors, professional expertise, and national policy
converging on one campus. It is doing for legitimacy exactly what the Southern
Pacific did for freight — mediating the traffic and charging for the passage.

**The mechanism.** Elite network reproduction, institutionalised. The chapter
names the thing the book has been circling: the university as an interface,
converting public research money and private wealth into personal authority, and
taking a position in the middle. Rail mediated commerce; Stanford mediates
succession.

**The key fact.** The Graduate School of Business was founded in 1925 — the year
Steinbeck left without a degree, and thirty-seven years before Phil Knight wrote
Nike as a class paper in one of its classrooms. The credential and the fortune
arrive in the same building.

**The human anchor.** Hoover as Secretary of Commerce, 1921–1928, running a
department that functions as a clearing house between industry and government,
and keeping his university connection live throughout.

**Excluded voices.** Everyone the interface screens out, which in the 1920s is
most of California. Also the university's own quotas and exclusions in this
period, which should be stated with specifics rather than gestured at.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the university operated as an interface
rather than merely an educator by showing donors, federal policy, and
professional accreditation routing through the same campus and the same people.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Two things happened at Stanford in 1925. The Graduate School of Business was
founded, and a student named John Steinbeck left without a degree. The chapter
puts them in the same paragraph and does not yet explain why.

Its subject is what Stanford became in the 1920s, which was something more
precise than elite. A credential is an instrument that lowers the cost of
trusting a stranger, and whoever issues one earns rent on every transaction it
enables. Through the decade, donors, professional expertise, and national policy
increasingly converged on the same campus and the same people, and the
university began functioning as a switchboard between private wealth and public
authority.

Hoover is the demonstration. As Secretary of Commerce from 1921 to 1928 he ran a
department that operated as a clearing house between industry and government —
standardising products, convening trade associations, allocating radio spectrum,
shaping civil aviation — while keeping his university connection continuously
live. Expertise flowed out to the state; state standing flowed back to the
campus. Named gifts and buildings accumulated, and what the money bought was not
only buildings.

The chapter draws the analogy the book has been preparing since Act I. The
Southern Pacific did not create the demand for freight; it charged for passage
across a position it controlled. An accreditation does the same thing to a
career. Rail mediated commerce, and Stanford was learning to mediate succession.

The cost is who the interface screens out, and the chapter gives specifics
rather than gestures: admissions practice in the 1920s, the quotas that
operated, and the composition of the campus in the year the business school
opened.

The interface is now operational. The next chapter walks out of it and looks
back, and the one after that tests it against a depression it cannot explain.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does an institution become a bridge between private money and public authority?
:::

Two things happened at Stanford in 1925. The Graduate School of Business was
founded, and a student named John Steinbeck left without a degree.

The chapter does not explain the second yet. It is about the first, and about
what the university had become by the middle of the 1920s, which was something
more specific than distinguished.

## What a credential is for

A credential is a device for lowering the cost of trusting a stranger.

Consider the problem it solves. An employer, an investor, or a government
department needs to know whether a person it has never met can do a difficult
thing. Direct assessment is expensive and slow. Reputation works only within a
community small enough for reputation to circulate. What a credential supplies
is a third party's assurance, standardised, portable, and cheap to read.

This is genuinely valuable, and the chapter is not sneering at it. An economy in
which strangers can be trusted at low cost is enormously more productive than
one in which they cannot.

It is also a position, and the position generates rent. Whoever issues the
credential is standing between a person and the opportunities that person could
otherwise only reach through personal connection, and the issuer's own standing
is what makes the instrument work. That is a chokepoint in the strict sense used
throughout this book, and the fact that it does useful work does not make it
something else.

Act I described the medieval university acquiring the licence to teach anywhere
and the Chinese state administering examinations at industrial scale. This is
the same instrument, in California, held by an institution that had been open
for thirty years.

## The switchboard

What distinguished Stanford in the 1920s was not the quality of its teaching. It
was the traffic.

Donors were becoming numerous and named. Buildings went up carrying the names of
the people who had paid for them, which is a transaction this book described in
Florence in Act I and will describe again in 2011.

Faculty moved into government service and back. Expertise flowed out to the
state, and standing acquired in Washington flowed back to the campus, and each
direction increased the value of the other. A professor who had run a federal
programme was a more valuable professor, and a university whose professors ran
federal programmes was a more valuable university.

And the graduates were beginning to occupy positions where they could hire the
next cohort, which is the point at which a network becomes self-sustaining.

Hoover is the demonstration case, as he is for most of this act. As Secretary of
Commerce from 1921 to 1928 he ran what had been a minor department as a national
clearing house — standardising industrial products, convening trade
associations, allocating radio spectrum, organising civil aviation, and
gathering statistics on a scale the federal government had not previously
attempted. It was government by convening rather than by regulating: bring the
industry together, produce a voluntary standard, and let the market enforce it.

He kept his Stanford connection continuously live throughout, as a trustee, as a
donor, and as the man whose name was on the library.

## The rail analogy, properly stated

Act I described the Southern Pacific charging what the traffic would bear
across a position it controlled. The comparison to a university is not
decorative and the chapter should make it precisely.

The railroad did not create the demand for freight. Farmers grew the crops;
markets wanted them; the railroad occupied the ground in between and priced the
passage. Its power came from being unavoidable rather than from being
productive, though it was also productive.

An accreditation occupies the same kind of ground. It does not create the
graduate's ability. It stands between the ability and the opportunity, and it is
unavoidable for anyone who wants access to the institutions that read it.

The difference is that a railroad's position is obvious and generates
constitutional conventions, while a university's position is regarded as a
public good and generates gratitude. This is the more effective arrangement, and
it is the reason Act I chapter 12 called the university a conversion of a
fortune into something that could not be regulated.

## Who was not there

The specifics matter more than the generality, so here they are.

Stanford in the 1920s operated an explicit cap on the enrolment of women, fixed
at five hundred by a decision of Jane Stanford's in 1899 and maintained in the
form of a ratio for decades afterwards. A university that had been coeducational
from its first day had, within a decade, limited the proportion of women it
would admit, and the limitation lasted into the second half of the century.

Black students were present in very small numbers and were excluded from most
campus housing and social organisations. Jewish students at elite American
universities in this period were subject to quotas that were sometimes explicit
and frequently effective without being written down.

And the university sat inside the residential geography described in the
previous chapter. Palo Alto and the surrounding towns operated restrictive
covenants; whoever could not buy a house within reach could not easily take a
job or a place within reach either.

The interface screened. That is what an interface does, and the chapter's
argument is not that Stanford was unusual among American universities in this
respect — it was not — but that the screening is the function rather than a
defect in it.

## Testing

The instrument that made mass credentialling possible arrived from a laboratory
on the same campus, and its inventor is the third Stanford figure in this act
whose work turns out to be about sorting.

Lewis Terman, professor of psychology at Stanford, published the Stanford-Binet
Intelligence Scale in 1916 — an American revision of Alfred Binet's French test,
which Binet had designed to identify schoolchildren needing additional help.
Terman's version did something different with it. It produced a single number
intended to represent a stable, largely inherited general capacity, and it was
designed for use at scale.

It was used at scale almost immediately. During the First World War the army
tested well over a million recruits using group instruments developed by Terman
and his colleagues, and the results were published and widely discussed. The
conclusions drawn from them about the relative capacities of national and racial
groups were used in the immigration debates of the early 1920s, and the tests'
cultural loading was obvious to critics at the time and was largely disregarded.

Terman was also an active eugenicist, which places him alongside Jordan in the
previous chapters, and he began in 1921 the longitudinal study of gifted
children that still bears his name and still runs.

The chapter's interest is structural. A standardised, cheap, apparently
objective measure of human capacity is precisely what a credentialling system
needs in order to scale beyond the point where individual judgment is possible.
The Scholastic Aptitude Test, first administered in 1926, descends directly from
this work.

The instrument that would sort American students for the next century was
developed by a professor of psychology at Stanford, and its author believed it
was measuring something hereditary.

His son Frederick, an engineer, becomes the central figure of this act's second
half.

## The business school

The Graduate School of Business opened in 1925, the second such school on the
west coast and among the earliest anywhere.

Its founding is worth marking because it formalises the credential as an
instrument in its own right. An undergraduate degree certifies general
capability. A graduate business degree certifies fitness for management
specifically, and it does so for people who have already been in the working
world — which means it functions less as education than as a re-sorting device,
a second gate that reassigns people who have already passed the first one.

In 1962 a middle-distance runner from Oregon with an accounting degree will take
a class in that school and write a paper about Japanese shoes. Act III chapter 6
is about what happened next.

## The interface is operational

By 1929 the machine has all its parts. Land that cannot be sold and can
therefore be leased. An endowment released from probate and appreciating. An
archive of world power in a library on the quad. Graduates in federal office.
Donors whose names are on the buildings. A business school issuing a second-
order credential.

And a student who arrived in 1919, accumulated ninety-three units over six
years, and walked out.
